title: How the Voyager Golden Records Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain the Voyager Golden Records, the gold-plated copper phonograph records aboard NASA's Voyager 1 and 2 probes, conceived largely by Carl Sagan with Frank Drake and Timothy Ferris and created by Linda Salzman Sagan and Ann Druyan's team. They trace the precursor Pioneer 10 and 11 plaques (the naked man and woman etching, the hydrogen hyperfine transition and pulsar map), the Lageos satellite message, the record's contents (greetings in 55 languages, 116 images encoded as audio, Kurt Waldheim's message, music from Bach to Chuck Berry, the sound essay including the human heartbeat and laughter, and the Music of the Spheres), the cover instructions and uranium-238 timestamp, and the controversy over the laughter's origin and the omitted Beatles tracks. Also includes a listener mail segment about Nazi gold.
topics: Beethoven Bach Chuck Berry Voyager record

segments.title: Opening banter and overview of the Golden Records
segments.summary: Hosts open with light banter about school dances, then introduce the two identical Voyager Golden Records aboard Voyager 1 and 2, the probes' distance from Earth, and the 1970s context of Carl Sagan's message-to-aliens project.

segments.title: Why the records were made and their durability
segments.summary: Discussion of the optimism of the 1970s space-messaging movement, whether it was a wise idea, the records' copper-and-gold construction and aluminum cover meant to last about a billion years, and the Voyager onboard computer memory.

segments.title: Pioneer 10 and 11 plaques
segments.summary: The precursor Pioneer plaque, sent on the Pioneer 10 and 11 probes, featuring a line drawing of a naked man and woman and the public outcry it caused, plus the friendly waving gesture and the map elements.

segments.title: Hydrogen transition and pulsar map
segments.summary: Explanation of how the Pioneer plaque used the hydrogen hyperfine transition as a universal unit of time and distance and a map of fourteen pulsars to locate Earth, credited mainly to Frank Drake.

segments.title: Lageos satellite message
segments.summary: Sagan's other message project, an inscription on the Lageos satellite showing the Pangaea continental arrangement and projected future continents.

segments.title: Choosing the record format and encoding images as sound
segments.summary: The decision to use a gold-plated copper LP played at 16 2/3 rpm for about an hour per side, and the use of Colorado Video's technique to convert television images into audio so pictures could be stored on the record.

segments.title: Cover instructions and uranium timestamp
segments.summary: The aluminum cover's instructions for playing the record and decoding images, including the test circle image, the pulsar map reused from the Pioneer plaque, and a uranium-238 piece used as a time stamp, plus the hosts' views on the difficulty of the task.

segments.title: Selecting images for the record
segments.summary: The 116 images chosen to show astronomy, biology, human life, nature, art and technology, with censorship of nudity into silhouettes, and the hosts' reaction to the collection's unsettling tone.

segments.title: Audio side: greetings, Waldheim message and languages
segments.summary: Side B's audio opens with a message from UN Secretary General Kurt Waldheim, followed by greetings in 55 languages, with notes on the Swahili omission and a child's English greeting from Nick Sagan.

segments.title: Music of the Spheres, sound essay and life signs
segments.summary: The whale song, the evolution sound essay including the heartbeat and laughter, the Music of the Spheres based on Kepler and recorded with Bell Labs, and the life signs EEG recording by Ann Druyan.

segments.title: Music selection and the laughter mystery
segments.summary: The music chosen from Bach, Beethoven, Chuck Berry, Blind Willie Johnson and Louis Armstrong, world music, the excluded Beatles and Dylan rumors, and the disputed identity of the laughter on the sound essay.

segments.title: Legacy of the project and Murmurs of Earth
segments.summary: The hosts assess the project as a hopeful, if imperfect, gesture, referencing Sagan's book Murmurs of Earth and closing thoughts on the records.

segments.title: Listener mail: Nazi gold
segments.summary: A listener from London writes that they are working on a legal case involving a Nazi gold legend mentioned in an earlier episode and sends an anonymous teaser.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and podcast production information.
